# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 39 (Bu-Vb Pc39)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc39
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 39
**Title (English, from literature):** Asking for fine foods
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Pācittiya 39 of the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, titled *Paṇītabhojana* ("Asking for fine foods"), establishes that a monk who is not sick and who solicits rich or luxurious food for his own consumption incurs a *pācittiya* offense [Hüsken 1997]. The rule specifies a canonical list of nine "fine foods" (*paṇītabhojana*): ghee (*sappi*), fresh butter (*navanīta*), oil (*tela*), honey (*madhu*), molasses (*phāṇita*), fish (*maccha*), meat (*maṃsa*), milk (*khīra*), and curd (*dadhi*) [Schmithausen 1991; Hüsken 1997]. As Lambert Schmithausen observes, although the rule penalizes expressly begging for fish and meat (Vin IV 88), the underlying rationale is not *ahiṃsā* but monastic modesty and ascetic decorum, as these items are grouped alongside dairy products and sweeteners [Schmithausen 1991]. The text is also cited in comparative studies of ancient Indian dietary ethics [Ulrich, Dietary polemics in South Asia]. In comparative vinaya analysis, Ute Hüsken demonstrates that this bhikkhu rule served as the direct template for the series of eight *Pāṭidesanīya* rules for nuns (Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pāṭidesanīya 1–8), which prohibit nuns from soliciting similar delicacies (omitting only fresh butter), an interrelation likewise discussed in the commentary *Samantapāsādikā* [Hüsken 1997].

 DharmaNexus aligns the text externally with Tibetan translations such as the *Bhikṣuṇīvinayavibhaṅga* (D 5) and the *Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati* (D 4104), as well as the Sanskrit *Śayanāsanavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus detects extensive textual reuse between this text and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pāṭidesanīya 1 and 2–8, as well as Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Sekhiya 37, Pācittiyas 31, 32, 56, and 57, and later commentaries including the *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā* [DharmaNexus]. An English translation has been produced by Bhikkhu Brahmali.
